name: Columbia
story:
Gold was found at Columbia on March 27, 1850. The gold lay in the surface gravels, but there was little water to wash them with, so miners built a network of aqueducts to bring it in, at a cost of more than a million dollars. Between 1850 and the early 1900s at least $87 million in gold came out of the surrounding hills.
The bedrock here is limestone, and limestone dissolves into knobs, pinnacles and deep potholes. The potholes held enormously rich gravel. Miners dug it out of the crevices and then washed the rest away with water cannons, and the pinnacles were left standing: the "rock gardens" that visitors walk among today.
In the lidar they are the rough, dark ground running south and east of the old town. The water-filled pit east of them is an old quarry in the same limestone; marble has long been quarried around Columbia. The long flat strip on the west side is Columbia Airport's runway.

sources.name: Columbia State Historic Park brochure (California State Parks)

name: Harvard Pit, Jamestown Mine
story:
The Harvard is the modern end of Mother Lode mining. Underground mines followed the gold here in the old days; from 1986 to 1994 Sonora Mining Corporation dug out the gold-bearing rock along the Melones fault from the top instead, in an open pit about 830 m long, 460 m wide and 185 m deep.
When mining ended, the pit began to fill. By November 2000 the lake was about 90 m (300 ft) deep. In 1998 and 1999 the USGS measured 720 to 1,100 parts per billion of arsenic in its water. Eleven evaporators now sit in the pit to keep the level down.
In the lidar the lake is a hole: laser light doesn't come back from water. North of it the waste rock stands in stepped dumps cut by haul roads, and the big flat oval to the west is the tailings facility. Its pond leaked, so it was drained, graded, capped with clay, covered with topsoil and seeded.

sources.name: Harvard open pit water (USGS Open-File Report 01-074)
Jamestown Mine tailings closure (Central Valley Water Board)

name: Rawhide Mine
story:
The Rawhide was one of the big underground mines of the Jamestown district, credited with about $6 million in gold. Its vein, of quartz and dolomite with gold and pyrite, was up to 70 feet thick between the walls, with an ore vein averaging 20 feet, and the main shaft followed it down the incline for 2,000 feet.
Around 1890 the district's lode mines took off, and in 1906 more than 300 stamps were pounding ore in its mills. Lode mining here ran until about World War I. Later development at the Rawhide, in 1921, proved worthless.
Underground mines leave less on the surface than pits and hydraulic diggings, so look for what came out of the hole: dumps of waste rock around the shafts, and the flat benches of old mill sites.
The long, smooth ridge curving across the east side is Table Mountain: a lava flow that ran down an ancient channel of the Stanislaus River about 10 million years ago and filled it. The softer ground around it has worn away, so the old riverbed now stands as an 18-mile, flat-topped ridge. The gold-bearing gravels buried beneath it were mined too.

name: Eagle-Shawmut Mine
story:
The Eagle-Shawmut, east of Chinese Camp, was a major Mother Lode mine, credited with about $7.4 million in gold. It worked on and off until 1892, then almost continuously (except for 1926 to 1936) until it shut down in 1947.
Its ore wasn't a rich vein but large low-grade bodies of pyrite-bearing ankerite and quartz, and of mariposite rock, streaked green with chromium mica. By 1940 the workings reached about 2,400 feet down and totalled some seven miles, and there was open-pit mining here by 1936.
The mill stood almost at the level of Woods Creek. Don Pedro Reservoir now fills that canyon, so in the lidar the water is a blank, and the old mill site is most likely under it. The USGS topo maps of 1947 and 1948 outlined tailings along the creek below the mine; on this map those outlines now lie out on the water.

sources.name: Eagle-Shawmut Mine (Western Mining History, from USGS MRDS)

name: Big Oak Flat
story:
Gold was found here in 1848 by James Savage, and the camp was first called Savage Diggins. It was renamed Big Oak Flat about 1850 for a giant oak in the middle of town, about 13 feet across. The tree was undermined in 1869 and burned in 1890; pieces of it remain.
The gravels at Big Oak Flat and Deer Flat were rich: they are credited with about $25 million in placer gold. Lode mining followed and kept going until World War I. About two miles northeast, the camp called First Garrote became Groveland.
In the lidar, look for the scars of the early placer work along the creeks and flats, and the dumps of the lode mines in the hills around town.

sources.name: Big Oak Flat historical marker, California Historical Landmark 406 (HMdb)
Big Oak Flat district (Oakland Museum of California)
